justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over longer horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to what would have been the prevailing market level, assuming mean-reversion dynamics dominate at short horizons and that no major scheduled catalysts were imminent. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with the long-run historical tendency of equity or commodity markets to trend upward over time. The one-month estimate continues that modest climb, though the incremental gain remains small because I was not incorporating strong directional signals — the forecast is essentially saying "things continue roughly as they are, with a slight upward bias."

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding of daily uncertainty over time. At one day, the interval is fairly tight because intraday and overnight volatility tends to be constrained in the absence of shock events. By one week, a broader range of macro data releases, central bank communications, and geopolitical developments can shift the market meaningfully. By one month, the uncertainty compounds further — earnings seasons, inflation prints, employment data, and shifting sentiment can all accumulate into quite large moves. The widths I chose roughly correspond to annualized volatility assumptions in the 15–20% range, which is a reasonable baseline for many financial assets.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these intervals entirely. On the downside, a sudden geopolitical escalation, an unexpected credit event or financial institution stress, a materially worse-than-expected inflation reading triggering aggressive central bank repricing, or a broader risk-off episode driven by deteriorating global growth data could all produce moves well below the lower bound of my one-month interval. On the upside, a surprise dovish policy pivot, a major positive geopolitical resolution, or a strong batch of corporate earnings could drive prices above the upper bound.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals, while probabilistically stated at the 90% level, are ultimately model-dependent and subject to parameter uncertainty. Fat-tailed distributions in financial markets mean that true tail events occur more frequently than normal-distribution assumptions would suggest. Black swan events — by definition unforeseeable — are the most important reason to treat any confidence interval with humility, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is simply more time for the unexpected to materialize.
